tests.title: links a captured plan to the open change, and the plan stands in for the approval of its changed requirements
does not link a plan to a closed change or one on another branch

claims.text: `change done` is refused unless the change is validated, or forced with a reason that the closed record keeps; `change abandon` needs a reason; a closed record is never edited by any change command and has no next step

tests.title: abandons with a reason, and a closed record is never edited by any change command
closes as done only when validated, or forced with a reason that is recorded

claims.text: A spike may write code before the spec and is never validated; `change convert <id> --to feature` is refused while it has no changed requirement or any changed requirement has no tagged test, and keeps the spike's trail when it succeeds

tests.title: lets a spike write code first, never validates it, and converts only with changed requirements and tests

claims.text: Two changes open on one capability and branch warn at start, are judged on the same changed claims, are each judged by their own run records, and a command that acts on one needs it named

tests.title: warns about a second change on one capability and judges both on the same changed claims

claims.text: `change report` builds the proof packet locally and marks it provisional: the requirements that changed in plain words with their local approval, the red-green sensitivity read from the run records, weakened tests, code changed under no change record, and no per-line list of unrequested code when no coverage was ingested

tests.title: builds a provisional proof packet of the requirements that changed and how far the proof got
names code changed under no change record and a weakened test

claims.text: The MCP server offers `specguard_change_start`, `_red`, `_green`, `_status` and `_report`, only status and report when read-only, and no tool that approves a requirement or closes, converts or abandons a change; the stage rules bind a tool call exactly as they bind the CLI

tests.title: offers the five change tools by default, no tool that approves or closes a change, and only status and report when read-only
starts a change, reports its stage with the next step, and refuses what the stage does not allow
returns the provisional packet as markdown followed by its JSON, and an error for an unknown change

claims.text: The hook entry answers a PreToolUse call on stdin with one JSON line and exit code 0: a deny or ask prints `hookSpecificOutput` with `hookEventName`, `permissionDecision` and the one-line reason, an allow that has advice (a warning, the back-at-red notice, a policy-file note) prints `additionalContext` and no `permissionDecision` so it never skips the user's permission prompt, and a plain allow prints nothing; the committed plugin bundle and `specguard hook pre-tool-use` print the same bytes

tests.title: prints a deny as hookSpecificOutput with permissionDecision and the reason, and exits 0
prints a warning as additionalContext without a permissionDecision, so it never skips the permission prompt
observe allows in silence and logs the decision
lets an open refactor change edit code at enforce
reads a Codex apply_patch payload and denies when any patched path is guarded

claims.text: The guard is silent, and writes and reads nothing, in a directory with no `.specguard/config.json`, for a path outside the repository, and for a tool or event it does not guard; it finds the project from a subdirectory and treats a path reached through a symlink to the repository as inside it

tests.title: is silent, and writes nothing, in a directory with no SpecGuard config
is silent for a path outside the repository and logs nothing for it
finds the project from a subdirectory
treats a path reached through a symlink to the repository as inside it

claims.text: A payload the entry cannot read, or an internal error, in a SpecGuard project allows the call with a one-line notice that CI still checks (`ERROR_OPEN`), exits 0 and is logged; the entry never throws

tests.title: fails open with a notice on malformed JSON in a SpecGuard project
allows a payload with an unknown tool or event without a word

claims.text: With `hooks.onError: "deny"` an error that stops the guard deciding (such as a config that no longer parses) in a project with an `enforce` capability denies with `ERROR_CLOSED`; the default is to allow, and an unreadable payload is always an allow

tests.title: an unreadable config allows with ERROR_OPEN by default, and denies with ERROR_CLOSED under hooks.onError deny
hooks.onError deny scaffolds the Claude guard with onFailure block

claims.text: The ownership index lists the files each capability owns, each capability's spec file, enforce level and source globs, the test globs, the specs and history directories, and every open change with its kind, capabilities, the test files its red run covered (the lock set), its red record's validity and whether its changed claims are approved against its base; closed changes are left out and a record that does not parse becomes a note, not an error

tests.title: lists owned files, capability globs, enforce levels, test globs and open changes with their locked tests
leaves a closed change out and turns a record that does not parse into a note, not an error
judges approvals of a feature change against its base: unapproved, then approved at the current wording
classifies a new file that matches a capability glob as owned, and a test file as a test

claims.text: The index is cached in `.specguard/cache/hook-index.json` under a stat-only fingerprint of the config, every spec and history file, every change record and every red record; it is reused while the fingerprint holds, rebuilt in process the moment a spec, record or the config moves, and not rebuilt for a test or source edit (new source files are matched by the capabilities' globs); a corrupt cache is a miss and the cache is written atomically

tests.title: build-index writes the cache and reports what it holds, and `index` is an alias
rebuilds a stale index in process: a spec raised to enforce binds on the very next call
the fingerprint moves with a spec edit, a new change record and a red record, and not with a test or source edit
caches the index, reuses it while the fingerprint holds, and rebuilds it when it does not

claims.text: Red validity is checked live: on every call the entry re-hashes the locked test files against the red record's tests hash, so editing a locked test makes red invalid without any index rebuild and restoring the file makes it valid again, and a red record that shows no failing test or ran on code that was not at base is never valid

tests.title: answers an edit to a locked test with the back-at-red message, then notices the edit through the live red check
re-hashes the locked tests on every call: an edit makes red invalid with no rebuild, restoring the file makes it valid again
a red record that shows no failing test, or ran on code that was not at base, is never valid

claims.text: The hook decides with no model and no network, in about 55 ms on a warm index (node start-up included) and under 200 ms when it has to rebuild the index for a small repository; the committed test allows a generous second

tests.title: answers well inside a second on a warm index

claims.text: Every decision except the silent ones is appended as one JSON line to `.specguard/cache/hooks.jsonl` with its time, session, agent, tool, paths, capabilities, level, code and change, and the log rolls over to `hooks.1.jsonl` past 1 MB, so it is bounded and never in git

tests.title: log lists the recorded decisions, and --denied only the denials
observe allows in silence and logs the decision
rolls the log over past 1 MB instead of growing without bound

claims.text: The plugin ships the guard as one committed self-contained file that imports only node built-ins, so it needs no install step, and a test rebuilds it from the sources and fails when the committed bundle differs, and the rebuild depends only on the sources, the dependency versions and the esbuild version, so hoisted npm, nested npm and pnpm installs produce byte-identical working bundles even when invoked outside the repository; distinct versions of a bundled package remain distinct

tests.title: builds identical working bundles with hoisted npm, nested npm and pnpm dependencies
keeps distinct versions and their labels when normalizing nested npm and pnpm layouts
equals a fresh build of the sources (run `npm run build:hook` after changing src/hooks or what they import)
is one self-contained file: it imports only node built-ins

claims.text: `specguard hook` has `pre-tool-use` (the same logic as the bundle, reading stdin), `build-index` (alias `index`: rebuild and cache the index), `doctor` (print the class of each path, or of a shell command, and what the guard would decide and why, as text or `--json`) and `log` (recent decisions, `--denied` for denials only)

tests.title: pre-tool-use prints exactly what the plugin bundle prints, for a deny, a warning and a silent allow
pre-tool-use is silent in a directory with no SpecGuard config
build-index writes the cache and reports what it holds, and `index` is an alias
doctor prints the class of each path and what the guard would decide, for a path and for a shell command
log lists the recorded decisions, and --denied only the denials

claims.text: A Codex session counts as an agent environment (`CODEX_THREAD_ID` is set), so the approve and lower guards apply, while an explicit `SPECGUARD_HOST_AGENT` setting still wins

tests.title: a Codex session counts as an agent environment, and an explicit SPECGUARD_HOST_AGENT still wins

claims.text: The edit guard treats any edit to an approval already on disk (a history entry whose frontmatter says `kind: approval`) as writing an approval and denies it, because an edit is judged on its new text alone and changing only the hashes in an existing approval would otherwise pass; other history entries stay editable

tests.title: denies an edit to an approval already on disk, even one that only changes a hash, and leaves other history alone

claims.text: A change walked end to end through the real commands and the real hook process obeys the order spec, approval by a person, tests, red, code, green: the guard denies a capability's code at `enforce` with no change open, then with unapproved requirements, then with no recorded red, allows it once red is recorded, and `change status` shows the change green and waiting for CI, never validated by itself

tests.title: walks spec, approval, tests, red, code, green and the stage lock, with the hook gating the code at every step

claims.text: The red evidence the edit guard reads is written by `change red` itself, in the same file and from the same run record `change status` reads: the file holds the run's per-test verdicts, the hashes the run saw and the test files it locks, so the guard and the stage detection cannot disagree about whether red holds

tests.title: a finished change is provisional on local evidence, certified only from CI evidence, and only then can the ratchet go to enforce
walks spec, approval, tests, red, code, green and the stage lock, with the hook gating the code at every step

claims.text: An agent cannot approve its own requirement by any route: `spec approve` refuses an agent environment, `history add` refuses approval entries, the guard denies a hand-written approval file, a rewrite of a change record and the shell forms of approving, and none of them moves a change out of the spec stage

tests.title: refuses `history add --kind approval`, and the hook denies a hand-written approval, a record edit and an approve command
walks spec, approval, tests, red, code, green and the stage lock, with the hook gating the code at every step

claims.text: Editing a locked test or a changed requirement after red sends the change back to the tests stage and the guard denies the code again until `change red` is run anew, which builds a tree with the owned code at base and leaves the working tree as it was; the guard announces the lock when a locked file is edited

tests.title: walks spec, approval, tests, red, code, green and the stage lock, with the hook gating the code at every step

claims.text: A refactor change opens only its own capability's code at once and needs no red, a requirement edit under it is reported as changing intent, and a spike may write code first but never reaches validated, not even with a passing CI verdict, and cannot be closed as done

tests.title: lets a refactor edit its own capability at once and no other, and refuses a requirement edit under it
lets a spike write code first, but a spike can never reach validated, not even with a passing CI verdict

claims.text: Two changes open on one capability are judged on the same changed claims and each needs its own red; any one with a valid red opens the code, and closing or abandoning it closes the code again unless the other has red

tests.title: judges both on the same changed claims; any one with a valid red opens the code; closing it closes the code again

claims.text: A finished change is `provisional` while its proof comes only from local runs and `certified` only from a CI proof note for a clean commit, and `enforce raise --to enforce` is refused on the first and accepted on the second even in a checkout that holds no local proof, after which the guard denies edits made without a change

tests.title: a finished change is provisional on local evidence, certified only from CI evidence, and only then can the ratchet go to enforce

claims.text: With a change open and red recorded, the guard answers from its cached index in under 200 ms at the median and 500 ms at the 95th percentile per call (a spawned process, node start-up included; about 50 ms on a quiet machine), for allow and deny alike

tests.title: answers from the cached index well inside the budget, for allow and deny alike

nodes.title: Local-first operation with an optional team server
nodes.value: SpecGuard works fully on one machine, and when a team server exists it also gives everyone shared proof from CI, shared documents and shared plans, without anyone depending on it.

claims.text: `specguard publish` writes one snapshot file holding the spec and history markdown, the trace model, the proof rows, the newest remediation plan and the contract graph, tagged with the project name, repository, branch, commit, origin and engine and hash versions; it never includes source code, working-tree files outside the spec tree, or prompts that were not committed as history, and it redacts credentials from every file; with `--push` or `--server` it also sends the snapshot to the project's team server, and a refusal or an unreachable server fails the command while the file is still written

tests.title: writes a snapshot a server would accept: specs, history, trace, proofs, and no source code [snapshot]
redacts credentials from every file and leaves the v1 archive out [redaction]
names the project from the flag, then config, then the directory [project-name]
rejects paths that leave the spec tree, non-markdown files and bad project names [paths]
rejects malformed, oversized and wrong-version input without throwing [malformed]
sends a large snapshot gzip-encoded, so a proxy with a 1 MB cap lets it through [gzip-push]
accepts a gzip-encoded snapshot, because proxies cap uploads at 1 MB, and refuses an expansion bomb or another encoding [gzip]

claims.text: A snapshot is validated before it is written or accepted: the project name is a safe identifier, every file is a markdown file inside the spec tree (no absolute paths, `..` or backslashes), the trace model has its required shape, an unknown version is refused, and anything over the size limit is refused

The API serves every project under `/api/v1/projects/:project/...`, lists projects at `/api/v1/projects`, and on a server with one project also serves the same routes without the prefix; a server with several projects answers an unprefixed route with a pointer to the prefixed form; besides the existing routes it serves specs with their file (and one spec's markdown), coverage per capability and unit, the document list, the contract graph and unresolved findings, and the web UI works under a path prefix and across projects

tests.title: serves one spec\'s markdown from the snapshot [spec-file]
is served under a path prefix, which only a plain path may be [base-path]
asks the server which projects exist, and uses the prefixed API when there is no default [projects]

claims.text: The API reports `apiVersion`, `engineVersion`, `hashVersion` and whether it accepts writes on `/health` and `/version`, so a client can refuse to mix incompatible data

tests.title: refuses a server that is not SpecGuard or speaks another API version, and flags other hash rules [versions]

claims.text: A registry that is not writable (the local `serve`) answers every write with 405; on a writable one a plan item is changed with `PATCH` by a signed-in maintainer, the change is attributed to them, a stale `If-Match` version is refused with 409 and writes nothing, and a lifecycle violation is refused with 422

tests.title: requires a token for plan changes made through the API, attributing them to its owner, and the CSRF header for browser sessions [writes]

claims.text: A team server keeps its state behind one backend interface (snapshots, plans per project, a document cache per project, tokens, an audit trail and model usage), implemented for files and for Postgres and held to the same contract tests; a project is shown from its newest snapshot on the default branch, else its newest overall; concurrent edits to plans lose nothing, with Postgres using a revision check and retry instead of row locks

tests.title: shows a project from its newest snapshot on the default branch, else its newest overall [snapshots-latest]
lists projects, knows which commits it has, and prunes the oldest [snapshots-housekeeping]
stores plans per project, lists them in order, resolves latest, and ignores a plan that does not validate [plans]
loses no update when many items of one plan change at once, and none when the update throws [plan-updates]
caches by namespace and slot per project, replacing an entry in place [cache]
finds tokens by hash, lets only the owner revoke, and tracks use [tokens]
keeps the audit trail and the model usage in order [audit-usage]
refuses a project name that could leave its directory or break a path [project-names]

claims.text: Every route except `/health` needs a credential: a token (a person's, a project's CI token, or the operator's bootstrap token) or, for browsers, the sandbox's signed-in user header, which reads and mints a person's own tokens but never grants an administrative power; a bad token is refused even when the header is present; a project-scoped credential reaches only its project; nobody mints a token more powerful than their own, admin tokens come only from the admin route; tokens are stored as hashes, shown once, revocable by their owner, and audited; changes made from a browser session need the `X-Requested-With` header

tests.title: serves health to anyone and everything else only to a valid credential [auth-gate]
is mounted under its base path and nowhere else [base-path]
refuses a request target that is not a valid path, and an oversized body [bad-input]
lets a signed-in user mint their own token, never more power than they hold, and revoke it [own-tokens]
reserves administration for an admin token: the header never grants it, and the bootstrap token does [admin]
records who made and revoked tokens in the audit log [audit]

claims.text: A project's CI token or a maintainer publishes a snapshot over HTTP, creating the project on first publish; the snapshot's plan is merged with the stored one, so statuses and tracker references that people set on the server survive a republish, an item marked fixed that a scan sees again reopens, and unresolved items the new plan lacks are kept unless that plan was made from the stored one

tests.title: accepts a snapshot from a project\'s CI token and serves the project from it [publish-and-read]
keeps a credential to its own project, and refuses viewers, bad snapshots and a mismatched name [publish-guards]
keeps what trackers changed when CI publishes a newer plan [plan-survives-republish]

claims.text: Documents on a team server are generated once per spec content, audience, prompt version and model and shared by everyone, and each generation runs in its own model scope with the requester's name, the project and the gateway's labels, so spend is attributed to the person who asked and recorded per user and project

tests.title: generates a document once for everyone, and attributes the model spend to whoever asked [docs-shared-and-attributed]

claims.text: The server fetches the `specguard-evidence` artifacts CI uploaded for each configured repository on a timer, publishes the snapshot inside under the configured project with the commit and branch taken from the workflow run, skips what it already has and artifacts that are expired, oversized, invalid or from forks, and reports one repository's failure without stopping the others

tests.title: publishes each new artifact under the configured project, with commit and branch from the run [publish]
does not fetch what it already has, and skips expired, forked, oversized and broken artifacts [skips]
reports a GitHub error for one repository and carries on with the next [error-isolation]
finds the snapshot wherever the upload put the archive root [zip-layouts]

claims.text: The server answers MCP over HTTP at `/mcp` for token holders only, as read-only tools (projects, system, capability, spec, audit, coverage, docs, history, findings, plans) that go through the same API as the same identity, so access rules, project scoping and redaction are the API's

tests.title: needs a token, lists read-only tools, and answers them through the API as the caller [mcp]
keeps a project-scoped token to its project even through MCP [mcp-scope]

claims.text: Commands that can use a server resolve it from config or the environment, check its health with a short timeout and a compatible API version, and otherwise behave locally: reads fall back silently and say which source they used; a shared write goes to the server or, with none, is written locally and marked local-only; a server that answers but refuses (bad token, no permission, lifecycle violation) is an error and never a quiet switch to local; `server.mode: required` makes an unreachable server an error and `off` never contacts it; `check --team`, the plan commands, the MCP plan tool and the VS Code extension all follow this, and a token saved by `login` is checked against the server before it is kept

tests.title: serves the workspace locally when no server is configured [no-server]
uses the team server when it is configured, healthy and has the project, with the token it was given [server]
falls back to the local server, with a reason, when the server is down, refuses, lacks the project or is another version [fallbacks]
never contacts a server when the mode is off, and lets the editor setting win over the project\'s [off-and-override]
reads the project\'s server block, names the project after the directory by default, and finds a token in order [resolve]
reports a command line that does not exist, and one that exits at once, instead of hanging [failures]
gives up when the server never says where it is listening [silent]
saves a token readable by its owner only, per server, and forgets it [save]
comes from config or the environment, takes the token from env or a saved login, and is absent when off [target]
connects to a healthy server, and returns null with the reason when there is none, in auto mode [auto]
treats an unusable server as an error only in required mode [required]
answers a slow server within the timeout by giving up on it [timeout]
sends the snapshot to the server and the project appears there [push]
fails, and says why, when the token is wrong, the server is down, or no server is configured [push-failures]
reads plans from the server when it answers, and from local files, saying so, when it does not [read-fallback]
reads locally, without trying a server, when none is configured [no-server]
writes to the server when it answers, and leaves the local plan alone [write-server]
writes locally and says it is local-only when the server does not answer [write-local]
does not hide a refusal by writing locally: a wrong token is an error and nothing changes [no-silent-switch]
writes locally when the plan has not been published yet, and reports a lifecycle violation instead of working around it [not-on-server]
shows CI\'s proofs set against this working tree\'s [lines]
says no server answered rather than failing [degraded]

claims.text: When `SPECGUARD_TRUSTED_PROXIES` lists addresses (exact, or IPv4 CIDR ranges) the sign-in header is honoured only from a connection that comes from one of them, so a container that reaches the server directly cannot sign in as anyone or become a maintainer by naming one; a token works from anywhere; the server warns at startup when it is not set

tests.title: matches exact addresses, IPv4 CIDR ranges and IPv4-mapped IPv6, and nothing malformed
ignores the header from a peer that is not the proxy, and still honours tokens from anyone
honours the header from the trusted proxy, and from anywhere when none is configured
reads SPECGUARD_TRUSTED_PROXIES, and warns at startup when it is not set

claims.text: The sign-in header never makes a maintainer on its own: without `SPECGUARD_TRUSTED_PROXIES` it signs in a read-only viewer whoever it names (it can read and mint viewer tokens, and cannot write, change plan items, define a workspace or mint a maintainer token), and only through a trusted proxy does naming a listed maintainer email make the session a maintainer; it is never an admin

tests.title: is a viewer without trusted proxies: it cannot write, and cannot mint itself a maintainer token
is a maintainer only through the proxy, where it can write and mint up to that role, and never an admin

claims.text: Each caller (the signed-in user, or the connecting address when there is no credential) is limited to a number of API requests a minute (600 for a signed-in caller, 60 with no credential), and the routes that can start a model call to fewer (30 a minute for `/docs/`); a caller over a limit gets `429` with `Retry-After`, a refused request is not counted, health is never limited, and the limits are set with `SPECGUARD_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN`, `_DOCS_PER_MIN` and `_ANON_PER_MIN`

tests.title: counts per caller over a sliding minute, says how long to wait, and does not count a refused request
holds document routes and credential-less callers to their own smaller limits
reads limits from the environment and ignores nonsense
answers 429 with Retry-After over HTTP, for a signed-in caller, a document route and a caller with no credential, but never for health
limits the routes that can start a model call more tightly than the rest

claims.text: The server keeps an audit trail of what changes through its API (token creation and revocation, plan item status changes, workspace definitions, published snapshots) with who did it, and of every refused attempt to change something (no credential, or a role too low) with the reason; reads are not recorded

tests.title: records who changed a workspace, and who tried to change one and was refused, and why
does not record a refused read, and writes no audit entry when the server is not asked to change anything

nodes.title: Test Strength
nodes.value: A claim counts as tested only when a real test that can fail is tagged to it, so skipped, gated or empty tests and weakened assertions are caught before they pass for proof.

claims.text: A test is classed `skipped` when its source marks it so: JavaScript `it.skip`, `xit`, `it.todo`, `test.fixme`, an enclosing `describe.skip`, a first-statement `test.skip()`, or a `.only` elsewhere in the file; Python `skip`/`xfail` decorators or `pytestmark`; Go `t.Skip` as the first statement; Rust `#[ignore]`; Java and Kotlin `@Disabled`, `@Ignore` or `@Test(enabled = false)` on the method or class

tests.title: maps extensions to languages
js: it.skip / test.skip / xit / it.todo / test.fixme are skipped with the right reason
js: tests inside describe.skip and xdescribe are enclosing-skip
js: a .only in the file makes the other tests focus-elsewhere
js: Playwright test.skip() as the first statement is skip-in-body
python: skip/skipif/xfail decorators, class decorators and module pytestmark
python: pytest.skip as first statement is skipped, inside if is conditional
go: t.Skip first is skipped, inside if conditional; testing.Short conditional; build tag file-wide
rust: #[ignore] skipped; #[cfg] conditional; assert_eq strong; unwrap-only weak; should_panic(expected) strong; assert!(true) trivial
jvm: @Disabled, @Ignore, @Test(enabled=false), class-level @Disabled are skipped
applyResultStatus(skip) turns strong into skipped/skip-result and keeps static reasons

claims.text: A test is classed `conditional` when it runs only under a condition: `skipIf`/`runIf`, a skip call inside the test, `skipif` decorators, `testing.Short()`, a Go build tag, Rust `#[cfg(...)]`, JUnit `@EnabledIf*`/`@DisabledIf*` or an `assume*` call, or a match of a regex in `testStrength.conditional` or the app's `test.conditional`; an invalid regex is rejected with an error

tests.title: js: skipIf, runIf and Playwright test.skip(condition) are conditional
config conditional regex matches body, declaration and file head; invalid regex throws
jvm: @EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable and Assumptions.assumeTrue are conditional
loads testStrength and the per-app test.conditional, and resolves them together
rejects a conditional that is not a valid regular expression

claims.text: A test with no assertion, or only trivial assertions such as `expect(true).toBe(true)` or `assert x == x`, is `weak`, and commented-out or quoted assertions are not counted

tests.title: js: expect(true).toBe(true) and expect(x).toBe(x) are trivial
js: a test with no assertion is weak/no-assertion and an unknown imported call alone does not count
js: commented-out assertions do not count, nor do assertions inside strings
python: assert True trivial; assert x is not None existence-only; assert a == b strong
unsupported extension is unknown/unsupported-language; unbalanced braces unparsable-body

claims.text: A test whose assertions only check that something exists, that nothing throws, or that an error occurred is `weak` with the reason `existence-only`, `no-throw-only` or `error-check-only`, and a test with at least one comparison, structural or exact assertion is `strong`

tests.title: js: a sole toBeDefined is existence-only; with toEqual it is strong
js: only not.toThrow is no-throw-only
js: a multi-line expect chain with resolves/not is detected
js: fc.assert sets property and is strong
js: wildcard matchers are counted
js: node assert, chai and ava styles are graded
js: regex literals, nested template literals and CRLF line endings do not derail body detection
python: pytest.raises with match is exact; self.assertEqual strong; assert_called_once_with strong
python: @given sets property
go: only if err != nil { t.Fatal } is error-check-only; if got != want { t.Errorf } strong
rust: proptest! sets property
rust: lifetimes and char literals do not derail brace matching
jvm: assertEquals strong; sole assertNotNull weak; assertThat(x) without matcher trivial
jvm: assertThatThrownBy(...).hasMessage strong; Mockito verify with literal args strong
kotlin: shouldBe strong; backtick method names
jvm: @Test(expected=) is throws; jqwik @Property sets property

claims.text: A test whose only assertions are snapshots is `weak` with the reason `snapshot-only` unless `testStrength.snapshotIsWeak` is false

tests.title: js: snapshot-only is weak by default and strong with snapshotIsWeak false

claims.text: A call to a same-file helper that asserts counts with the helper's strength to a depth of three, a call to a convention-named helper such as `expectValidUser` counts as strength 2, a name in `testStrength.assertHelpers` counts as strength 3, and any other imported call counts for nothing

tests.title: js: same-file helper with expect counts; helper chains to depth 3
js: convention helper expectValidUser counts at strength 2; config helper at 3
js: a same-file helper that asserts nothing is not rescued by its name
python: same-file helper and snake-case convention helper count

claims.text: A claim is meaningfully tested when, for each required layer except `functional`, at least one tagged test at that layer is strong, or when no layer is required and at least one tagged test is strong, and otherwise the result lists why: no tagged tests, all skipped, conditional only, weak only, a named layer not meaningful, or strength unknown

nodes.title: Workspaces - Multi-Repo and Monorepo
nodes.value: Teams that split one system across several repos or packages can treat it as one system, so a change in one place shows what else must be re-checked.

claims.text: A workspace manifest at `.specguard/workspace.json` lists repos with a path and a role of consumer, provider, test or docs, an optional description, and an optional catalog directory; it is found by walking up from any child directory and unknown fields are preserved

A missing manifest is a clear "not found" configuration error and an invalid or schema-failing manifest is a configuration error; repos without their own SpecGuard config load with no config rather than failing

`workspace init` registers sibling repos that have a SpecGuard config, deriving each repo key from the directory name alone and each role from the repo's contents (test frameworks, UI or server dependencies, API schema files, language markers) and never from a platform-specific name; it never overwrites an existing manifest and fails with guidance when no repo is found

claims.text: The contract graph is stored in `.specguard/contracts.json` as nodes (a spec in a repo, identified `<repo>::<specPath>`) and directed edges from consumer to provider with a type of graphql, rest, iframe, upload, event, test or docs, a surface list, a last-verified time and a source

`contracts` builds edges from structured contract blocks in spec Dependencies sections, from importers supplied by enabled plugins and, only with `--with-llm`, from free-text dependencies of specs that have no structured block; lines that do not match the format are skipped

Building the graph is idempotent and incremental: existing edges are preserved and surface items merged, `--force` rebuilds from scratch, `--repo <key>` restricts to one repo, validation problems such as an edge naming a missing node are warnings that do not fail the command, and the file is written atomically

`impact` accepts a node id, a workspace-relative path or an absolute path, walks consumers breadth-first to a depth limit (default 6), separates direct from transitive consumers with the connecting edge type and surface, and `--upstream` also lists the providers the target depends on

`impact` suggests a drift command for each affected consumer repo and an "update docs" suggestion for docs-type edges, reports "no downstream consumers" with exit 0, and exits 1 with an example id format for an unresolvable target or with guidance when no graph exists; it never modifies files

`workspace drift` finds repos with changes since a git ref (default the previous commit), maps changed files to graph nodes, runs drift in the affected consumer repos for the dependent specs, supports `--force` and `--repo`, and exits 3 when any consumer has drifted
A claim can be referenced across repos as `repo:specKey#claim` (or `specKey#claim` within the current repo), so a journey or proof can depend on a claim in another repo

claims.text: Detection also covers Go (`go.work`), Cargo workspaces and uv workspaces besides JavaScript ones, and a repo may hold several; `init` writes one app per ecosystem over every package's sources plus a units manifest carrying each package's test command, instead of one app per package, with glob negations kept at the front

tests.title: reads go.work, in block and single-line forms, with each module\'s name [go-work]
reads go.work when a comment follows a single-line use or holds a closing paren [go-work-comments]
reads Cargo workspace members, globs and exclusions [cargo]
reads uv workspace members [uv]
a pyproject without a uv workspace is not a monorepo [no-uv]
lists the packages of every ecosystem in a polyglot repo [polyglot]
writes one app over every package and a units manifest with each package\'s test command [one-config-units]
gives each ecosystem of a polyglot repo its own app, the primary language first [polyglot-apps]

claims.text: `check` reports each unit's source files, unowned files and the capabilities touching it (a capability spanning packages appears in each, and gets one drift verdict); `test run` runs each package unit's own command, only named units with `--unit`, or with `--affected [--since <ref>]` the changed units plus every unit that depends on them, running everything when a changed file is outside every unit; `serve` exposes the rollup at `/api/v1/units`, and security plan items carry the unit key

tests.title: maps changed files to units and reports files outside every unit [files-to-units]
adds every unit that depends on a changed one, transitively [dependents]
names the workspace unit each finding is in, and omits it outside a workspace [unit-key]
reports each unit with its source files, unowned files and the capabilities that touch it [check-units]
serves the same rollup over the API [api-units]
runs every unit that says how to run its tests, and ingests the results [all-units]
--unit runs only the named units and rejects an unknown one [unit-filter]
--affected runs the changed units and everything that depends on them, and nothing else [affected]
a change to a leaf unit tests only that unit [affected-leaf]
runs everything when a changed file is outside every unit, since it could affect any [affected-outside]
runs nothing when nothing changed, and compares against a ref with --since [affected-none-since]
fails, running nothing, when git cannot list the changes, instead of reporting green [bad-ref]
maps changes to units when the workspace root sits below the git root [subdirectory-root]

claims.text: Dependencies between units, read from each unit's own manifest (package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml), become `package` contract edges with source `workspace`, rebuilt on every `contracts` run so a removed dependency disappears; `impact` accepts a unit or a file inside one, and reports the capabilities with code in the affected units as well as the units themselves

tests.title: reads JS, Go, Cargo and Python manifests and ignores external packages [deps-by-ecosystem]
reads Python dependencies that carry extras, and Go modules without a dot in their path [extras-and-dotless]
records where the dependency is declared and never makes a unit depend on itself [declared-in]
builds an edge for each dependency between units, from their own manifests [package-edges]
rebuilds them every run, so a removed dependency disappears and nothing duplicates [regenerated]
reports the units downstream of a package and the capabilities built on them [impact-capabilities]
accepts a file inside a package as the target, and a change nothing depends on has no downstream [impact-target-forms]

claims.text: A repo or unit entry may carry `ignore: true` (with an optional `ignoreReason`); loading the manifest moves every ignored entry out of `repos` and `units` into `ignored`, so every workspace pipeline (contracts, impact, drift, trace, test run, security, proofs, rollup) skips it without a check of its own, a key listed under both `repos` and `units` is still rejected, and `workspace ignore|unignore <key>` edits the raw manifest without normalising it

tests.title: moves an ignored repo out of repos and units so every pipeline skips it
still rejects a key listed under both repos and units, ignored or not
ignore and unignore edit the manifest on disk without normalising it

claims.text: Workspace-level commands take `--workspace <path>` or `SPECGUARD_WORKSPACE`, naming a `workspace.json`, its folder, its `.specguard` folder or a `.code-workspace` file (read as JSON with comments); a `.code-workspace` keeps its manifest in `<its folder>/.specguard-workspaces/<name>` unless its `specguard.workspaceManifest` setting says otherwise, and per-repo state such as the proof ledger never follows the flag

tests.title: reads JSONC: comments, trailing commas and unnamed folders
gives each .code-workspace its own manifest folder unless a setting points elsewhere
accepts a workspace.json, its folder, the .specguard folder or a .code-workspace
uses the flag, then SPECGUARD_WORKSPACE, and nothing when neither is set

claims.text: `workspace sync` and `workspace init --from <file>` register the folders of a `.code-workspace` as repos (key from the folder name, role from the repo's contents, identity by real path), add folders with no SpecGuard config as ignored with reason `auto:no-config` and lift that ignore once a config appears, report folders missing on disk, remove or ignore folders that were dropped, and never change an entry it did not create or a field edited by hand; `workspace init --recursive` searches nested folders and stops at a repo

tests.title: adds each folder, ignoring the ones with no SpecGuard config
is a no-op the second time
lifts an automatic ignore once the repo gets a config, but never a hand ignore
never overwrites a hand edit, and never touches entries it did not create
removes a folder that was dropped if untouched, else ignores it
reports a folder missing on disk and does not add it; a repeat is not a removal
keeps two folders with the same name apart
syncs a real manifest on disk from a JSONC .code-workspace and leaves package units alone
finds nested repos, stops at a repo, and skips hidden folders and node_modules

claims.text: The workspace rollup combines, per repo and in total, what each repo has recorded: coverage, claims proven, failed, stale and unproven, claims by test layer, open security items by severity from the newest plan, documentation freshness and intent gaps (recorded in the trace by `check`), with a state that says why a repo has no numbers; ignored repos are listed and add nothing to the totals

tests.title: reports coverage, claims and open security items from what a repo recorded
says why a repo has no numbers instead of reporting zeros as fact
carries git-derived gaps recorded in the trace, and counts layers claim by claim
lists ignored repos but adds nothing from them to the totals
reads a manifest of real folders: configured, unconfigured, ignored

claims.text: `check --workspace [path]` prints the rollup and writes `.specguard/rollup.json`; with `--refresh` it first runs `check` in each active repo; the exit code is the worst per-repo outcome (validation failed, drift, missing specs)

tests.title: exits with the worst per-repo outcome in check\'s own order

claims.text: `serve --workspace [path]` serves every active repo as a project and the rollup at `GET /api/v1/workspace`, read-only

tests.title: serves each active repo as a project and the rollup at /api/v1/workspace

claims.text: A team server keeps named workspaces (a set of projects, each with a key, a role and an ignore flag; file and Postgres storage) defined with `PUT /api/v1/workspaces/<name>` by a maintainer with an unscoped token, readable at `GET /api/v1/workspaces[/<name>]`, and `GET /api/v1/workspaces/<name>/rollup` combines each project's newest snapshot the way the local rollup does (a project with no snapshot shows as `no-trace`, ignored projects are listed and not counted); a token limited to one project may not define a workspace and sees only one made of that project alone

tests.title: stores workspaces: create, replace, read back, list in name order, and refuse a bad name [workspaces]
a maintainer defines a workspace, anyone signed in reads it, and the rollup combines each project\'s newest snapshot
refuses a workspace from a viewer or an anonymous caller, bad names and bad bodies, and 404s an unknown one
a token limited to one project cannot define a workspace and sees only one made of that project alone

claims.text: `workspace publish [--name n] [--server url]` defines the workspace on the team server from the manifest: each repo is named by the manifest's `server.projects` map, else its own `server.project`, else its folder, ignored repos are flagged, and a missing server or a refusal is reported and fails the command; each repo still publishes its own snapshot

tests.title: names each repo by the manifest\'s map, else its own server.project, else its folder, and flags the ignored
puts the workspace on the server found in a repo config, and says so when none is configured or the server refuses

claims.text: `contracts --with-llm` says before it sends anything that only each spec's Dependencies section goes to the model (and to which provider and model), lists each spec it sends, and stops at `--max-llm-specs` (default 50), naming the specs it did not send

tests.title: sends only the Dependencies text of each spec, says so and lists them, and stops at the cap
sends nothing without --with-llm, and defaults the cap to 50

claims.text: A per-user `~/.config/specguard/.env` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/specguard/.env`) supplies keys to every workspace and repo on the machine at the lowest precedence, below the repo's and the workspace's file and below real environment variables

tests.title: fills in what the repo, the workspace and the shell left unset, and loses to all three
reads no user file when the environment names no home or config folder

claims.text: `specguard key set` saves the model API key (`llm.apiKeyEnv`, default `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) into the user's, the workspace's or the repo's `.env` with mode 600, reading it from a hidden prompt, stdin or `--from-env` and never from an argument, replacing an existing line, refusing a multi-line value, and never printing the key; `key status` says which files define it without showing it; `config.json` only ever names the variable

tests.title: saves a key piped on stdin to the user file with mode 600, replaces it later, and never prints it
reports where the key is set without showing it
writes the repo scope into the repo and leaves other lines alone, and refuses a multi-line value

claims.text: When `.specguard/.env` (which holds secrets) is readable by other users the CLI warns, names the file and the fix (`chmod 600`), never prints a value, and still loads the file

tests.title: warns when other users can read it, names the fix, and still loads it; says nothing when it is private

claims.text: `workspace sync` treats a folder with no config of its own but covered by an overlay as a normal repo unit instead of `auto:no-config`, recording `configVia: overlay` in an optional unit field (manifests without it load unchanged), and the workspace scan, rollup and role guess read its config, trace and proofs from the overlay; a git root folder whose overlay entry names an app folder inside it counts as covered, while a monorepo root whose apps each have an entry (ambiguous) does not

tests.title: registers a folder with no config of its own but covered by an overlay as a normal repo, recording configVia
drops configVia when the overlay no longer covers the folder, and a second sync is a no-op
an overlay registered after the first sync lifts the auto ignore on the next one; the manifest stays loadable
workspace init scanning, the rollup and the role guess all see an overlay-covered repo as configured
treats the git root folder of a repo whose overlay entry names an app inside it as covered; a monorepo root with two apps is not

claims.text: A unit that sync marked `auto:no-config` is retired automatically on the next sync once an overlay covers it, and `configVia` is dropped again when the overlay stops covering it; a unit a person marked ignore by hand (any other reason, or an entry sync did not create) is never touched

tests.title: retires an auto:no-config ignore when an overlay now covers the unit, and never touches a hand-made ignore
an overlay registered after the first sync lifts the auto ignore on the next one; the manifest stays loadable
